The benchmark US stock measures were mostly pointing higher before the opening bell Monday as traders await a busy week of corporate earnings and key inflation data.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.1% in premarket trading, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.1%. Equity markets finished Friday trading with weekly gains.

Wall Street banking giants JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Bank of America (BAC), Morgan Stanley (MS), Goldman Sachs (GS), Wells Fargo (WFC) and Citigroup (C) are expected to release their latest financial results this week, along with major corporations such as Johnson & Johnson (JNJ), UnitedHealth (UNH) and Charles Schwab (SCHW).

Investors also await the September consumer price index scheduled to be out on Wednesday, while data on wholesale prices and retail sales for the same month are due Thursday.

Treasury yields trended higher early Monday, with the two-year rate up 3.5 basis points to 4.79% and the 10-year rate up 0.9 basis points to 5.24%.

Last week, a preliminary survey of the University of Michigan showed that consumer sentiment fell to a five-month low in October as the one- and five-year inflation expectations reached their highest levels since May.

"Consumer sentiment dropped for the third consecutive month in October, with elevated gas prices and higher borrowing costs making consumers more worried about current economic conditions," Oxford Economics US Economist Grace Zwemmer said in remarks emailed to MT Newswires on Friday. "Both year-ahead and long-run inflation expectations ticked up, highlighting consumers' affordability concerns."

West Texas Intermediate crude oil inclined 0.9% to $92.67 a barrel, while Brent gained 0.8% to $105.64.

In a Truth Social post on Sunday, President Donald Trump announced Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire, with immediate effect. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of violating the energy ceasefire after a strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, Reuters reported Monday.

Last week, Trump said on social media that Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply diesel to the US and global markets.

Trump also told reporters on Saturday that the US may join Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels following an attack on Riyadh's international airport, according to CNBC. "We're going to look at it," Trump reportedly said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is ready to provide assistance to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militants, according to Al Jazeera.

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack is slated to speak at 12:50 pm ET.

Spot gold dipped 0.3% to $4,203 per troy ounce, while bitcoin decreased 0.2% to $83,435.

Stack of cigarettes by Andrii Shablovskyi via iStock

Rate worries are back. On Oct. 7, the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.36%, its highest level in 24 years. Fresh Fed minutes added fuel, showing most policymakers thought another rate hike before year-end made sense. Stocks didn't take it well; the S&P 500 ($SPX) slipped 0.22%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ($DOWI) fell 0.66%, and the Nasdaq 100 ($IUXX) gave up 0.21%.

That kind of market usually sends investors hunting for steady cash flow and fat dividends, and tobacco stocks check both boxes. Altria Group (MO) sits at the center of that trade. The company bumped its quarterly dividend by 4.7% in August, from $1.06 to $1.11 per share, and MO stock is up more than 24% so far in 2026.

More News from Barchart

'When You Say I Should Pay $100 Billion, Then I'm Starting To Do A Little Math': Bill Gates Said He'd Happily Pay 'Over $10 Billion In Taxes' But Some Are Asking Too Much

How to Play Rivian Stock as RIVN Keeps Falling Despite Record Deliveries

Dan Ives Calls SpaceX's $40B Nvidia Chip Debt Plan a 'Smart Move'

Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines.

But there's a catch. Higher yields give investors other places to earn income, so Altria has to work harder to justify its risks. With Altria's Oct. 29 third-quarter earnings report around the corner and management guiding for 2026 adjusted EPS of $5.61 to $5.72, does MO stock still offer enough income and growth to be worth owning as rate fears build? Let's take a closer look.

www.barchart.com
Altria's Fundamentals Face the Market Test

Altria's Q2 results showed that its pricing power is still doing the heavy lifting as cigarette demand shrinks, although the quarter wasn't perfect. Revenue excluding excise taxes rose 1.2% year-over-year (YOY) to $5.36 billion, which was in line with the $5.35 billion analysts expected, while adjusted EPS climbed 2.8% to $1.48, just shy of the $1.50 forecast.

Operating margin also slipped to 58.6% from 61.1% in the year-ago period. Still, first-half adjusted EPS rose 4.9% to $2.80. Altria also handed nearly $3.9 billion back to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. That was enough for management to lift the low end of its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.61 to $5.72, good for 3.5% to 5.5% growth.

Altria is also looking for savings beyond price hikes. In August, the company's Philip Morris USA unit signed a contract-manufacturing deal with non-U.S. affiliates of Philip Morris International (PM), with first shipments expected in early 2027. The tie-up could make manufacturing more efficient, cut costs, and open doors to international nicotine markets, although management says it won't move the needle on 2026 results. For now, any further upside this year comes down to delivering on guidance and investors sticking with its defensive income story.

title: Stock futures mixed ahead of bank earnings, CPI data

Stock futures mixed ahead of bank earnings, CPI data
Quartz · Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images

U.S. stock futures pointed to a mixed open Monday, with investors looking ahead to a week packed with major bank earnings and key inflation data.

S&P 500 futures were up 0.1%, with Dow Jones Industrial Average futures adding 53 points, or 0.1%, while Nasdaq 100 futures edged down 0.1%. U.S. bond markets are closed Monday for Columbus Day.

Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley, and Wells Fargo are all expected to report third-quarter results this week, according to CNBC. September consumer price index data is due Wednesday, followed by the producer price index on Thursday. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is also scheduled to appear Thursday at an IMF and World Bank summit in Bangkok, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The S&P 500 is on track to post 29.6% earnings growth for the third quarter, which would mark the fourth consecutive quarter of above-25% growth, according to CNBC, citing FactSet's John Butters. Still, what executives say about the pressure from higher fuel and borrowing costs is likely to draw more investor attention than the reported figures themselves.

"Investors have kind of narrowed in on some of the important aspects," Brian Leonard, portfolio manager of the Keeley Gabelli Small Cap Dividend Fund, told CNBC. "Can this company withstand what's happening? Pass along, continue to grow margins, and the future is going to be better than the most recent past."

The week begins against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty. Over the weekend, President Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine and unveiled a diesel supply arrangement under which Russia would release an initial 300,000 tons of fuel. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy quickly accused Moscow of breaking the ceasefire, and traders largely shrugged off the news, in part because the diesel volume involved — below a single day of U.S. consumption, according to the Journal — was seen as too small to move markets meaningfully. Brent crude was up roughly 1% in early trading, and diesel futures dipped.

Trump separately said he was weighing whether the United States should join Saudi Arabia in operations against Houthi militants backed by Iran following a lethal strike on Riyadh's main airport over the weekend.

Wall Street is coming off a positive week. Both the Dow and S&P 500 ended the week in the green for the second time in three weeks, and the Nasdaq Composite extended its winning streak to four consecutive weeks, lifted by strength in technology shares.

European indexes rose broadly in early trading. South Korea's Kospi fell 3.65% and the Kosdaq dropped 4.83%. Markets in Japan were closed for a holiday.

Iren shares jumped more than 5% after The Information reported that the data center operator signed a multi-year AI cloud services deal with Anthropic. Stellantis shares also climbed after the European Union and China reached an understanding that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said following two days of talks in Beijing. The "shared understanding" would "moderate" exports of hybrids and plug-in hybrids and reduce imports by several million cars over four years, though Sefcovic did not say how it would be implemented.

Meanwhile, Micron Technology shares slipped 2.1% after Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies reported progress on a next-generation DRAM design that could raise storage density and intensify competition with South Korean rivals. Shares also faced pressure from a Taiwanese union's demand that Micron direct 15% of operating profit to quarterly employee bonuses, an arrangement the company has declined to formalize. Micron employs roughly 15,000 workers at its Taoyuan and Taichung sites, more than 80% of its Taiwan workforce.

Investing.com -- Asian stocks were mixed on Monday as South Korean shares tumbled on renewed competition concerns in the memory-chip market, while oil retreated amid uncertainty over a proposed Russia-Ukraine energy truce.

The KOSPI fell 3.5%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 0.2% and China's CSI 300 slipped 0.8%.

Trading was thin on Monday, with Japan's cash equity markets closed for Sports Day and U.S. bond markets shut for Columbus Day. U.S. stock exchanges remained open, while Treasury cash trading was suspended for the holiday.

Wall Street extended its record-setting week on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 0.6%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 0.8% and the Nasdaq Composite rising 0.6%.

In Asian trade, Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.2% to 31,163.25 and S&P 500 futures gained 0.2% to 7,877.75.

Markets are looking to U.S. consumer and producer inflation data and retail sales figures this week for clues on the Federal Reserve's next moves. Markets price an 18% chance of a Fed rate hike this month and an 85% probability of an increase in December.

Korean chipmakers fall as CXMT advances memory technology

South Korea's KOSPI slumped as trading resumed after a long weekend, with SK Hynix falling 2.6% and Samsung Electronics losing 2.3%. LG Innotek plunged 13.1%.

The pressure followed progress reported by Chinese memory-chip maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) in its 4F² DRAM architecture, which is designed to increase memory density.

Not finding the right stocks? Our AI's list of investor-grade stock picks for October just dropped »

CXMT is targeting a year-end launch for next-generation DDR5 server-memory modules, potentially intensifying competition with Samsung and SK Hynix in the higher-value server-memory market. TrendForce reported that the design could increase memory density by 30%-50%.

Other technology shares were mixed. Largan rose 8%, Foxconn gained 2.6% and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing slipped 0.4%.

Attention is also turning to TSMC's results on Thursday, with analysts expecting a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings, driven by AI-chip demand and advanced CoWoS packaging. Consensus forecasts point to third-quarter net profit of T$746.3 billion ($23.4 billion), up 65% year-on-year.

Geely Automobile rose 2.5% after announcing plans to enter Canada, with its first vehicle sales targeted for 2027.

Meanwhile, China and the EU reached a 16-point consensus on trade, investment, export controls and intellectual property, with Beijing agreeing to curb hybrid-car exports as the bloc considers safeguard measures.

MAAS tumbles as Firmus IPO cancellation rattles AI investment

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.8%, but MAAS Group fell 11.2% to A$4.11, extending losses after AI data-centre operator Firmus cancelled its planned $5 billion IPO.

Oil retreated after an early advance. Brent crude fell 1.3% to $103.38 a barrel, while U.S. crude declined 1.7% to $90.29, both remaining below recent highs. Weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on shipping and Riyadh's main airport renewed fears of a broader regional conflict and further energy-supply disruptions.

President Donald Trump's claim that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire remained unconfirmed by either side. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no agreement had been finalised, while Trump's proposal for Russia to increase diesel exports drew objections from Republican and Democratic senators, who questioned whether it could be illegal.

Elsewhere, the NZX 50 gained 0.6% to 13,827.62, Singapore's Straits Times rose 0.3%, and Indonesia's Jakarta Composite fell 1.9%. India's Nifty 50 fell 0.7%, while the Sensex lost 0.8%.

Third-quarter earnings will test whether corporate profits can sustain equity valuations as financing costs rise. Major U.S. banks begin reporting on Tuesday, ahead of TSMC's results on Thursday.
